Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

edits.note: the brainstorm is bounded by the share-out that follows it, and the five expected answers (boat, bridge, ferry, stepping stones, swimming) stand

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud twice at a natural, expressive pace, pausing at each stanza break. Students follow in their textbooks (pp.27–28) without speaking.
Teacher reads aloud a third time, inviting students to join in softly on the repeated phrase 'prettier far than these.' Attention is drawn to the two stanzas and how each ends on the same line.
Students read aloud in pairs — one reads stanza 1, the partner reads stanza 2 — switching roles once. Teacher circulates, modelling pronunciation of 'overtops' and 'heaven'.

Whole-class read: all voices together, teacher conducting the pace. Teacher asks: 'What two things is the poet comparing in stanza one? What two things in stanza two?' Students respond orally; no written record expected yet.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the poem's first encounter: the goal is sound and rhythm, not comprehension analysis. Students who are unfamiliar with the word 'bow' may think of an archer's bow; hold that thought for the word-meaning discussion in a later sitting rather than rushing it now.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the two refrains on the board — 'prettier far than these' and 'But…' — and asks students to locate each in their books (pp.27–28). Brief discussion: how many times does each appear?

Choral reading in two halves: one group reads the 'statement' lines (boats/bridges), the other reads the 'but' lines. Groups swap roles after one full run. Teacher claps the beat to keep rhythm steady.

Students practise reciting stanza 2 from memory in small groups, checking against the text. Emphasis placed on a slight rise in voice at 'But the bow that bridges heaven' and a deliberate slowdown at 'builds a road from earth to sky'.

Three volunteers recite the full poem aloud to the class. Class offers one positive observation after each — what sounded confident, clear or expressive. Teacher closes by naming the literary device of repeating 'prettier far than these' as a kind of echo (epistrophe) in simple terms.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the poem read aloud in a previous encounter, students are now ready to feel its rhythm in their own voices. The anaphoric 'But' lines carry the poem's turn; make sure students hear and feel the pause before each 'But' rather than rushing through it.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (pp.27–28): discuss meaning of 'bow' and which bridge the poet prefers.

time_bands.activity: Quick paired chant of the poem (pp.27–28) to warm up voices. Teacher then asks: 'The poem uses the word bow — what does it mean here? Is it the same as an archer's bow?'

Class discussion on Let us Think A questions 1 and 2 (p.28): the meaning of 'bow' as the arch of the rainbow, and why the poet prefers the rainbow-bridge over man-made bridges. Students give reasons from the poem's own words ('bridges heaven', 'builds a road from earth to sky').

Discussion of question 3 (p.28): what does 'these' refer to in each stanza? Teacher guides students to track back through the stanza — 'these' in stanza 1 = boats and ships; 'these' in stanza 2 = man-made bridges. Students note answers briefly in their notebooks.

True/False set from question 4 (p.28) — teacher reads each statement aloud; students write T or F on a slip of paper and hold it up. Class compares answers and corrects misunderstandings immediately with reference to the poem text.

periods.teacher_notes: The pronoun 'these' in question 3 is the trickiest comprehension move in the poem: each stanza sets up its own referent, and students often assume 'these' means the same thing both times. Pausing to track back through the stanza before answering is the key habit to model here.
materials: Slips of paper for True/False responses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.28): discuss crossing rivers, seeing rainbows, and imagining a rainbow walk.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the first prompt from Let us Think B (p.28): 'What are the ways in which you can cross a river?' Students brainstorm in pairs, then share with the class — boat, bridge, ferry, stepping stones, swimming.

Second prompt (p.28): 'Have you ever seen a rainbow in real life or in pictures? How did you feel?' Students describe their experience or an imagined one. Teacher encourages full sentences and models one response: 'I saw a rainbow after a heavy shower and it looked like someone had painted the sky.'

Third prompt (p.28): 'If you could walk on a rainbow, where do you think it would take you?' Students share imaginative responses in a guided open circle. Teacher gently pushes for reasons — 'Why there? What would you see?'

Teacher draws the discussion back to the poem: 'Rossetti says the rainbow builds a road from earth to sky — now that you have imagined walking one, does that image feel real to you?' Students respond briefly. Teacher closes by asking one student to re-read the poem's final three lines aloud (p.28).

periods.teacher_notes: The open imaginative prompt about walking on a rainbow links personal experience to the poem's central metaphor of the rainbow as a road. Encourage students who have not seen a real rainbow to draw on pictures or paintings — the prompt explicitly allows this.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.30): listen to words read aloud, give five rhyming words for each.

time_bands.activity: Students arrange chairs in a circle (or sit in a circle on the floor). Teacher explains the task: 'I will say a word. You will give five words that rhyme with it — words that end with the same sound. Ready?' Teacher demonstrates using 'ship → chip, trip' as the textbook example (p.30).

Teacher reads each word aloud clearly and slowly — Ship, Tree, Bow, Rain, Sun, Sea — pausing after each for students to respond with rhyming words in turn around the circle. Teacher accepts any phonetically valid rhyme; students clap when a word rhymes correctly.

Continuing around the circle with Sail, And, Sky, Far (p.30). Teacher reads each word three to four times before moving on if students need more time. When a student offers a near-rhyme, teacher models the correct sound contrast gently.

Quick debrief: teacher picks three or four words from the set and asks the class to call out their favourite rhyme for each. Teacher notes which sounds (e.g. '-ow', '-ar') produced the richest responses and celebrates the breadth of the class's word knowledge.

periods.teacher_notes: This task focuses on sound, not spelling — accept any phonetically valid rhyme regardless of how the child might spell it. For the word 'And', students may initially find rhyming harder; accept 'hand', 'sand', 'band', 'land', 'grand' as all valid and model one if the circle stalls.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.30): recite 'Colours' and 'Aachoo!' in happy, angry, and surprised voices.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads 'Colours' aloud once (p.30) in a neutral voice, then immediately reads it again in a clearly happy voice — smiling, light, warm. Students notice the difference. Teacher asks: 'What changed in my voice? What did I do with my tone, speed, and face?'

Students recite 'Colours' in groups of four — first in a happy voice, then (on teacher's signal) in an angry voice, then in a surprised voice. Teacher circulates and models each mood if a group seems uncertain. Swap groups so every student has a turn leading.

Same three-voice exercise with 'Aachoo!' (p.30) — this poem's elephant story lends itself to a big, surprised 'AACHOO!' moment. Teacher invites one group to perform the poem dramatically for the class in all three voices sequentially.

Brief class discussion: which voice felt most natural for each poem and why? Teacher connects back to Rossetti's poem — 'If we were to recite The Rainbow, which voice would fit its mood — happy, angry, or surprised? Why?' Students give reasons.

periods.teacher_notes: The purpose of the three-voice task is to make students physically aware that the same words carry different meaning depending on tone, pace, and pitch — a foundation for expressive recitation. The 'angry' voice often produces the most laughter; channel that energy into the surprised voice for 'Aachoo!'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.29): unscramble letters to find words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the solved example on the board: 'sial → SAIL' (p.29). Class reads the solved word, finds it in the poem, and reads the line it appears in aloud. Teacher explains: every scrambled word below is a word from the poem — finding it in the poem is a valid checking strategy.

Students work individually on the first five scrambled words — vierr, sae, oduscl, risebgd, nhveea (p.29) — writing the unscrambled form next to each. Teacher circulates; for any student stuck, the hint is: 'Check the poem line by line.'

Students complete the remaining three — eoptvros, owb, droa (p.29). Pairs check each other's answers. Teacher then reveals each answer on the board and asks a volunteer to find the word in the poem text and read its line aloud each time.

Quick whole-class oral round: teacher calls out a word (e.g. 'heaven') and students race to recall which line of the poem it comes from. Four or five words are quizzed. This closes the activity by embedding the words back in their poetic context.

periods.teacher_notes: The scrambled words in this task are all drawn directly from the poem, so the text itself is the answer key — encourage students to use the poem as a reference rather than guessing blindly. 'Eoptvros' (overtops) is the longest and most challenging; students unfamiliar with the word should be guided to find it in stanza 2 before unscrambling.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.29): spin-the-finger game — respond to poem-exploration prompts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the Let us Learn B activity (p.29): students sit in pairs; one traces a finger in a slow circle above the five labelled segments while the partner says 'Stop.' The finger's position determines the prompt to respond to. Teacher reads all five prompts aloud so students know what they might land on.

Pairs play two rounds each, responding to whichever segment the finger lands on. Teacher circulates and listens — prompting where needed: for 'rhyming pairs', guide students to 'rivers/these', 'seas/please/trees'; for 'repeated words', point to 'prettier far than these' and the 'But' anaphora.

Whole-class share: teacher calls on one pair per prompt (covering all five). The 'new title' responses are written on the board for the class to read and comment on. The 'musical instrument' prompt generates a brief creative discussion.

Teacher closes by asking the class to identify the two most repeated structural features of the poem — the 'But' at the start of key lines and 'prettier far than these' at the end of each stanza. Students say them aloud together to feel the poem's architecture.

periods.teacher_notes: This game-format task builds literary awareness through play rather than formal analysis: students encounter rhyme, repetition, imagery, and title-thinking without the weight of written tasks. Validate all creative 'new title' suggestions — even unusual ones open a good discussion about what the poem is really about.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write D (p.36): write opposites starting with S; make sentences using them.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the given example on the board: 'large × small' (p.36). Teacher asks: 'What makes small the opposite of large? Now, can you think of any other word whose opposite starts with S?' Students brainstorm two or three examples orally before opening the book.

Students work through the ten opposite pairs in Let us Write D (p.36) — weak, fast, rough, dull, curved, finish, addition, complicated, mild, blunt — writing the S-word opposite next to each. Teacher circulates; for 'complicated × simple' and 'addition × subtraction', offer a context clue if students are stuck.

Students choose any four of their S-word answers and write a sentence for each in their notebooks. Teacher models one: 'The road from earth to sky in Rossetti's poem seems straight, not curved.' Students try connecting at least one sentence to the poem's theme.
Pairs swap notebooks and read each other's sentences. Each reader picks the sentence they find most interesting and reads it to the class. Teacher collects a few striking examples on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes produce near-opposites rather than true opposites (e.g. 'slim' for 'large'). Redirect by asking: 'If something is large, is something slim its complete opposite, or just a different size?' The constraint that answers begin with S is a game-like scaffold — treat it as fun rather than a stressful rule.

periods.activity_title: Colours in the Kitchen — Spice Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write F (p.37): identify colours and mother-tongue names of kitchen spices.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'The poem celebrates colour in the sky. What colours do we find in our own kitchens?' Students name spices they know. Teacher introduces the nine spices from Let us Write F (p.37) — clove, cinnamon, dry chilli, garlic, curry leaves, peppercorns, fennel seeds, cumin seeds, mustard seeds — and places any real or illustrated examples on the demonstration table if available.

Students fill in the table (p.37): for each spice, they write its colour and its name in their mother tongue. Teacher moves around to check colour descriptions — cinnamon is brown, curry leaves are dark green, dry chilli is red, mustard seeds are yellow-black, etc.

Class share: teacher calls each spice name; students respond with the colour they have written. Where there is variation (peppercorns can be described as black or dark grey; fennel seeds as pale green or light yellow-green), teacher affirms that descriptions can differ and discusses why.

Students share the mother-tongue names in turn — this naturally surfaces the richness of different languages in the classroom. Teacher connects back to the poem: 'Rossetti saw colour in clouds and rainbows; we find colour in our own everyday world, even in the kitchen.'

periods.teacher_notes: This task genuinely varies by classroom — the mother-tongue column will have different languages depending on who is in the class, and that variation is a feature. If real spices are not available, the textbook's colour descriptions and common knowledge are sufficient; do not feel that specimens must be sourced.
materials: Real or illustrated spice specimens if available

periods.activity_title: Writing About a Journey — Guided Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.31): write an 80–100 word paragraph about a journey to a place visited recently.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the poem: 'Boats and ships travel across water to reach new places — have you ever travelled somewhere? Today we write about one journey.' Teacher reads aloud the six suggested content points from Let us Write A (p.31) — time, destination, purpose, companion, likes/dislikes, local food/landmark — and asks students to choose which points they will include.

Planning phase: students spend a brief, focused time jotting down four or five words or phrases for each point they have chosen — not sentences yet, just memory prompts. Teacher circulates and helps students who cannot recall a journey to choose a day trip, a visit to a relative, or even a local market visit.

Drafting: students write their 80–100 word paragraph in their notebooks. Teacher models a short opening sentence on the board: 'Last summer, I travelled to Mysore with my family to visit the famous Mysore Palace.' Students write their own opening line first, then continue.

Two or three volunteers read their paragraph aloud. Peers listen and offer one observation: 'I liked the detail about ___.' Teacher checks that each paragraph has an opening (when/where), a middle (what happened/liked), and a closing (how it felt). Students make a quick self-check mark against each section in their draft.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not travelled far may worry their journey is 'too small.' Reassure the class that a visit to a nearby temple, market, or grandparent's village is a perfectly valid journey — the writing task values detail and description, not distance. The six content points are prompts, not a required checklist.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p.34): complete the compound-word table using word pairs and pictures.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'rain + bow = rainbow' on the board (p.34) and asks: 'What kind of word is rainbow? It is made of two smaller words joined together — we call these compound words.' Teacher models two more: 'sun + flower = sunflower', 'note + book = notebook.' Students say the compound word aloud as the teacher writes each.

Students open the textbook to Let us Write B (p.34) and work through items 2–10. For items where a picture clue is given in the textbook (teacup, wristwatch, armchair, earthworm, tablecloth, notebook, earring, toothpaste), they use the picture as the main clue. Teacher circulates and confirms: 'The picture IS the answer — just name what you see.'

Pairs compare their completed tables and discuss any disagreements. Teacher reveals answers on the board one by one, asking a student to write each compound word. Class reads each compound word aloud and claps on the join between the two parts: 'WRIST — WATCH', 'ARM — CHAIR'.

Students try to generate three compound words not in the table — from the classroom, from the poem, or from their own lives. Each student shares one. Teacher lists a few on the board. Students copy the full list of compound words from the board into their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: The textbook page carries small picture clues beside each row; make sure students know to use the picture as the primary clue for items where both word-parts need to be filled in. Students often confuse compound words with phrases — 'post office' or 'ice cream' are useful contrast examples to show the difference.

periods.activity_title: Words as Nouns and Verbs — Sentence Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write C (p.35): write two sentences for four words — once as a noun, once as a verb.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the worked example from Let us Write C (p.35): 'bridge' as a noun ('I have seen a bridge made of roots in Meghalaya') and as a verb ('Some planks of wood were used to bridge the stream'). Class discusses: in which sentence is 'bridge' a thing? In which is it an action? Students point to the verb and noun in each sentence.

Students choose four words from the list — cut, bat, picture, cry, filter, dance, plant, paint, fly, face (p.35) — and write one noun sentence and one verb sentence for each. Teacher circulates; if a student writes 'The bat is flying' (noun used but described with a verb), guide them: 'Is bat the thing or the action in this sentence?'

Partners exchange notebooks and check: for each sentence pair, they underline the chosen word and write N (noun) or V (verb) above it. If they disagree, they discuss before calling the teacher. Teacher moves between pairs to mediate.

Class share: teacher calls out three words from the list; for each, two students read their noun and verb sentences. Class decides whether the word has been used correctly. Teacher corrects gently on the board if a sentence is unclear.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common confusion here is writing a sentence where the target word is used as one part of speech but described doing something that makes it sound like the other — 'The fly flew' is technically correct (fly = noun) but students often doubt themselves. Use the question 'Is it a thing or an action in this sentence?' as the consistent checking question.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Flowerpot Friend and Mixing Colours

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write G (p.38): design and colour a Flowerpot Friend.
Let us Do (p.39): complete colour-mixing activity and name the new colours.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the Flowerpot Friend examples in the textbook (p.38) — three completed characters. Students observe how each flowerpot has been given a personality through accessories, expression, and colour. Teacher invites: 'Who will your Flowerpot Friend be? Give it a name and a personality before you start drawing.'

Students design and colour their own Flowerpot Friend on the blank outline (p.38) or on a sheet of drawing paper. Teacher encourages decoration with patterns, accessories, and colour combinations. Students who finish early write a one-sentence character description beside their drawing.

Students turn to Let us Do (p.39) — six colour-mixing challenges. Teacher reads each combination aloud: 'red + blue = ?' Students work out and write the new colour name (filling the partial spelling), and if colouring materials are available, colour the result blob. Class verifies each answer together orally.

Gallery moment: students hold up or lay their Flowerpot Friend drawings on the desk. Teacher connects colour mixing to the poem — 'The rainbow is nature's greatest colour display; you have just been working with colour too.' Two students share their Flowerpot Friend's name and personality aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The two tasks in this sitting share a theme of colour and creativity, making them natural companions. If coloured pencils or crayons are not available, students can describe the colours they would use in words beside each blob in the Let us Do activity — the vocabulary learning is the same.

periods.activity_title: Boats and Rainbows — Explore and Discuss

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore A & B (p.40): boats research and presentation; human-made vs. natural things group discussion.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Let us Explore A (p.40): 'The poem begins with boats and ships. How many types of boats can you name?' Class brainstorms — rowboat, canoe, catamaran, steamboat, houseboat, ferry, sailboat, fishing boat. Teacher writes responses on the board.

Students work in groups of four. Each group chooses three boat types from the board list, draws a quick sketch of each, and notes two differences between them (size, use, power source, where used). Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Is it used on a river or the sea? Is it powered by wind, engine, or human effort?'

Let us Explore B (p.40): class splits into two groups. Group 1 discusses human-made things — ships, bridges, roads — what they are for, how they are built, what materials are used. Group 2 discusses natural things — clouds, rainbows, rivers, sky. Each group organises three points to share.

One spokesperson from each group presents their three points. Class discusses: 'Which group's examples feel more impressive to you — and which does Rossetti's poem say is prettier?' Students vote by show of hands, then teacher closes with the poem's final two lines read aloud: 'Is prettier far than these.'

periods.teacher_notes: Students researching boats have access only to class knowledge at this point — the task is designed for brainstorming and discussion, not library research during the sitting. The human-made vs. natural discussion in Explore B mirrors the poem's own structural argument and is a good place to see how well students have absorbed Rossetti's comparative logic.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Rossetti used comparison throughout the poem — boats vs. clouds, bridges vs. rainbow. In one sentence, what is her main message?' Students respond orally; three or four share. Teacher then invites the whole class to recite the poem from memory (or with minimal help from the book), paying attention to the rising emphasis at each 'But.'

Quick-fire word round: teacher calls out a word from the poem — 'bow', 'overtops', 'heaven', 'epistrophe', 'compound word', 'opposite'. Students give a definition, example, or sentence drawn from what the chapter covered. This recaps vocabulary, grammar, and literary awareness together.

Students write a five-to-seven line poem of their own using the poem's comparative structure: 'A ___ does ___, / But the ___ / Is prettier far.' Teacher provides the opening frame on the board. Students fill it with any nature-versus-human-made comparison they choose — it may be in the sky, on land, or in the sea. Students write and complete within the sitting.

Three volunteers read their poems aloud. Class listens and identifies: Where is the 'but'? What is being compared? What is the final verdict? Teacher closes by asking: 'Isaac Newton showed that white light hides all the rainbow's colours inside it — what does Rossetti show us that we might miss in ordinary things?' Students give final thoughts.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the poem's comparative logic, the chapter's vocabulary and grammar work, and the creative and observational activities — naming all of those by their content rather than by which sitting they occurred in. The student poem in the third band is a fresh, brief task: it begins and ends here, modelled on Rossetti's own structure.

items.item_stem: In the second stanza of the poem, Rossetti calls the rainbow 'the bow that bridges heaven.' Which of the following best explains what the word 'bow' means in that line?

options.label: A
options.text: A boat that sails on a river

options.label: B
options.text: A knot tied on a ribbon

options.label: C
options.text: A weapon used to shoot arrows

options.label: D
options.text: The curved arch of the rainbow in the sky

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has taken the most familiar meaning of 'bow' without reading the context of the sky and heaven.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student is thinking of everyday ribbon-bows rather than the poem's imagery of a great arch in the sky.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misreading that confuses the poem's water imagery in stanza one with the sky imagery in stanza two.

items.source_lo: Student identifies textual evidence and traces pronoun reference using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two-stanza poem; 'bow' as rainbow metaphor; pronoun 'these' shifts referent per stanza.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the word 'these' appears at the end of both stanzas in the phrase 'prettier far than these.' Explain what 'these' refers to in stanza one and what it refers to in stanza two. Use details from the poem in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: In stanza one, 'these' refers to the boats that sail on rivers and the ships that sail on seas. In stanza two, 'these' refers to the man-made bridges built on rivers.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will say two words aloud. Listen carefully. Choose the pair of words that rhyme with each other.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student may be matching by meaning (both are things in nature) rather than listening for the same end-sound.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student has not yet distinguished the '-ow' and '-y' sounds as different endings.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a focus on the poem's topic (rain and bridge both appear) rather than on the sound pattern of rhyme.

items.item_stem: Recite the second stanza of 'The Rainbow' by Christina Rossetti aloud. First recite it in a quiet, wondering voice as though you have just spotted the rainbow. Then recite it again in a joyful, excited voice. Your teacher will listen for clear pronunciation and a change in tone between the two readings.

expected_elements: Audible difference in tone between the two readings.
Deliberate pause or emphasis before 'prettier far than these'.

items.item_stem: The poem 'The Rainbow' describes how boats and ships journey across rivers and seas. Imagine you are a boat sailing on a wide river. Write three to four sentences describing your journey — where you are going, what you can see on either bank, and how the water feels beneath you.

expected_elements: Names a destination or direction of travel.
